checkpoints: Calling `SwaggerModule.createDocument(app, config)` inside a request handler means the full controller/DTO metadata scan and OpenAPI document assembly reruns on every single hit to that route, which is why an idle service shows rising CPU the moment something polls the endpoint repeatedly.

The generated OpenAPI document is a deterministic function of the code currently deployed in the running process — two requests handled by the same process, with no code change between them, can never produce a different document, so recomputing it per request just recreates a byte-identical artifact N times.

Because the expensive scan-and-assemble step yields the same output for the lifetime of a process, that work belongs at startup (or memoized on the first hit) rather than inside the request path; after that, serving the spec is nothing more than returning an already-built object.

The fix is to call `createDocument` exactly once during bootstrap, hold the resulting document, and have the route return that held object instead of rebuilding it — moving one function call out of the request handler removes the entire per-request scan.

Using `SwaggerModule.setup("swagger", app, document)` instead of hand-wiring the JSON route lets one generated document back both the human-readable UI at `/swagger` and the raw JSON at `/swagger-json`, so there is one artifact serving multiple surfaces rather than duplicated generation logic.

The document only changes when the code changes, and a code change requires a new build and a fresh process that runs bootstrap again — so generating the spec at startup is exactly as fresh as generating it per request, just at a fraction of the cost, which is the direct answer to "but what if the spec needs to change?"

There is no runtime scenario where a live, already-booted process needs to serve a newer spec than the one produced when it started, since nothing about its own routes or DTOs can mutate without a redeploy.

Correctness of the fix is verified by checking that the `/swagger-json` response body is byte-identical before and after the change, that latency and CPU flatten to the cost of serving a cached object even under continuous polling, and that after an actual code change plus redeploy the served document reflects the new schema — proving the switch to startup generation never sacrificed freshness.
In an UpdateUserDto where every field is marked optional, a client that omits a field causes that field to arrive at the handler as `undefined`, not as something the handler can treat as "skip this."

Assigning a payload field directly onto the entity row without checking whether it was actually present applies full-replace semantics to a route meant to only touch what changed — the omitted field gets overwritten with `undefined`, and the ORM persists that as `null`, wiping previously stored data.

PUT and PATCH differ in write scope: PUT is a full replacement where the client sends the complete representation and the server can assign every field directly, while PATCH is a partial update where the server must write only the fields present in the payload and leave everything else untouched.

The fix is a per-field presence check before assignment — e.g. `if (payload.name !== undefined) row.name = payload.name` — so a field absent from the payload keeps its previously stored value instead of being cleared.

Adding a "keep the old value if the field is absent" fallback to a genuine PUT handler is the mirror-image bug: it lets omitted fields silently survive a request that is contractually supposed to overwrite the whole resource, breaking PUT's replace-everything guarantee.

Verifying the fix requires checking both directions independently: PATCH with a partial body leaves the untouched field unchanged, PUT with a full body overwrites every field, and resending that same PUT payload again converges the resource to the same state, which is the idempotency property both PUT and PATCH are expected to have.

The presence-check strategy is representation-dependent: an `!== undefined`/null check works when the language distinguishes "absent" from "a real value," but in languages where an absent field arrives as a zero-value (e.g. an empty string in Go), the same strategy needs a different signal — a pointer type or an explicit presence map — to distinguish "not sent" from "sent as empty."

A plain undefined/null presence check cannot distinguish "field was never sent" from "field was sent as null/empty specifically to clear it" — supporting an intentional clear operation requires an extra signal beyond simple presence checking, such as a sentinel value or a separate "fields to clear" list.

Two error shapes coming out of the same API for what is conceptually the same kind of failure (an error) usually means two different code paths are handling errors, not one - the discriminator is a property of how each error is routed, not randomness or client-side parsing.

A parameterized `@Catch(HttpException)` scopes a filter to only intercept exceptions that are instances of that specific type - it does not act as a global safety net for everything an application can throw.

A plain `throw new Error("boom")` is not an instance of `HttpException`, so it never matches a filter scoped with `@Catch(HttpException)` and is never routed to that filter at all, regardless of the filter being registered globally.

An exception that bypasses a type-scoped filter falls straight through to the framework's own built-in default exception handler, which builds its own response body in a different shape and, depending on configuration, can surface the raw error message or a stack trace directly to the client.

Making the catch registration unconditional (a parameterless `@Catch()`) turns the filter into a true catch-all so no exception type can structurally bypass it, closing the gap that let plain runtime errors slip through.

Once the filter is a catch-all, it must branch internally: when the caught value is an `HttpException`, its real status and message are preserved and returned as before; otherwise the response is hardcoded to a generic 500 with a generic message, while the actual exception and its stack trace are logged server-side only, never included in the response body.

An exception filter functions as the single border deciding what error information leaves the system, so preventing leaks has to be a structural property of that boundary's scope rather than a hope that every handler always throws a recognized, deliberately-shaped error.

Correctness after the fix is confirmed by three checks together: the previously-leaking endpoint now returns the same envelope shape with a generic message and no internal string; a genuine `HttpException` such as a 404 still returns its original status and details unchanged; and the real error plus its stack trace still appears in server logs, showing nothing was silently swallowed - only hidden from the client.

Copying an entire raw request body directly onto a persistence entity (mass assignment) lets a client set fields the API never intended to accept — for example flipping an `isAdmin` flag to true through one extra key in the payload — which is a privilege-escalation vulnerability, not a cosmetic issue.

The fix for mass assignment is a declared boundary contract — a DTO listing only the fields the endpoint is meant to accept — enforced as an allowlist (e.g. a validation pipe configured with `whitelist`/`forbidNonWhitelisted`) so unknown fields are stripped or the whole request is rejected before it ever reaches the persistence layer.

Reusing the persistence entity itself as the input type merges the wire contract with the storage shape, so any column added later for internal bookkeeping (like an admin flag) automatically becomes a client-writable input field.

Manual inline validation — scattered if-statements invented per handler — drifts over time, tends to miss real rules such as email format checking, and produces inconsistent, ad hoc error messages across different endpoints.

Declarative validation (decorators such as `@IsEmail`, `@MinLength`, `@Min`) combined with one global validation layer applied to every route produces consistent, structured error responses and removes the need to hand-roll checks per handler.

A nested object field, such as an address, is persisted with no deep validation unless the contract explicitly declares nested validation for it, so an invalid nested value is silently stored instead of surfacing an error with a specific field path like `address.zip`.

A query parameter that looks numeric is still a string on the wire; without explicit type coercion, a comparison such as `age >= minAge` compares a number against a string and can silently misbehave instead of throwing an error.

Verifying a fix for these problems means confirming that an unexpected extra field is rejected or stripped rather than persisted, that a bad nested field returns an error carrying its correct nested path, that a numeric-looking query parameter now compares correctly, and that a previously valid payload still behaves exactly as before.

In a prompt-safety pipeline, redacting PII before the injection scanner runs wastes redaction work on prompts that are about to be blocked anyway, and it makes the block decision incidentally depend on the redaction step having executed first — a dependency that should not exist. The injection scan should run first, against the raw prompt, before any redaction happens.

Wrapping the injection-scanner call in a try/catch that logs a warning and then calls the LLM provider anyway on any exception is a fail-open design: the exact moment the scanner is broken or throws is the moment the entire safety gate silently becomes a pass-through, forwarding the raw, unredacted prompt straight to the provider.

Of the violations in such a pipeline, the fail-open catch around the scanner is the most severe because it is silent and total — any runtime exception converts the whole gate into a bypass, and a log line like "scanner failed, continuing" reads as a benign warning rather than signaling that the safety layer just failed, so no one gets paged for it.

Because redaction runs before the scan, a scanner failure forwards a prompt that has already been redacted, which makes the response look "safe-ish" even though the actual security control — injection detection — never ran at all; the two violations compound each other.

Writing the full raw prompt into the audit log when a request is blocked, "for debugging," copies any PII that prompt contains into every log aggregator and retention policy that engineers with log access can reach — a second, unintended exposure of the exact data the pipeline exists to protect, even though nothing left the process to an external provider.

A fail-closed fix means any exception during the scan step must result in a blocked response (or be rethrown to a global filter that returns an error status), never a fallthrough to the provider call — "I don't know if this is safe" has to be treated the same as "this is unsafe," not the same as "this is safe."

Audit logging on a blocked decision should record only the decision and evidence — such as the matched finding kinds — never the raw prompt text; on a successful forward, only the already-redacted prompt should be logged, never the original raw input.

Proving such a fix requires tests showing: a prompt containing both an injection phrase and PII is blocked with zero calls to the provider and no redaction warning, proving order; forcing the scanner to throw results in a blocked response and never a forwarded one, proving fail-closed behavior; and captured log output for both a block and a forward never contains the raw PII substring from the input, proving the log boundary holds.
